title: Bismuth-magnesium sample said to be from Roswell, found in an army officer's grandfather's archives
summary: Jesse Michels tells of Bismuth-magnesium sample said to be from Roswell, found in an army officer's grandfather's archives, about 1947 at Roswell, New Mexico, and relays what a named person told them. As told, not a fact.

tellings.quote: Long story short, this army officer was going through his grandfather's archives when he found this rare sample. And then written in the diary was that it was a piece from uh Roswell.
looked at the magnesium bismuth piece from roswell which was i guess a grandfather who was a colonel in the roswell cleanup collection this was sort of left in the safe and the grandson found it
tellings.difference: This telling makes the grandfather a colonel in the Roswell cleanup and says the piece was left in a safe, where the story has it in archives with a diary note, and it credits nobody rather than Hal Puthoff.
tellings.link_reason: Both tellings are about the same bismuth-magnesium sample said to come from Roswell 1947, which a grandson found among his grandfather's belongings.

tellings.difference: This telling puts the piece with Garry Nolan at Stanford, where Michels saw it during a visit, and it does not mention Roswell or the army officer's grandfather's archives.

plain: A small piece of layered metal made of magnesium and bismuth is said to come from Roswell, New Mexico, where a strange craft is reported to have crashed in 1947. Michels passes on what he was told: an army officer going through his grandfather's archives found the sample, and "written in the diary was that it was a piece from uh Roswell". The physicist Hal Puthoff tells it a little differently. He says it "was sent anonymously by someone claiming to be an army officer". In another version Michels makes the grandfather a colonel in the Roswell cleanup and says the piece sat in a safe. The sample is now with Garry Nolan, a Stanford scientist, and Michels says he saw it during a visit to Nolan's lab. Elsewhere Michels says the bismuth layers are "less than a human hair" thick, and that "nowhere could we find any evidence that anybody ever made one of these". He also links the piece to the researcher Jacques Vallée and guesses that it might allow magnetic levitation. If the story holds, it would be a physical scrap of a craft no one on Earth knows how to build.
